newsitem.title: JAPAN: Economists see Japan growth, but no solid recovery.
newsitem.headline: Economists see Japan growth, but no solid recovery.

text.p: Japan's economy is expected to have grown steadily in the last three months of 1996, but economists polled by Reuters said it was still too early to judge whether solid recovery had really taken hold.
"The figures themselves will confirm that the economy is steadily expanding," said Tatsushi Shikano, an economist at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics Inc.
"But we won't know about the real economic conditions and whether the recovery is solid until we look at data for April-June and July-September period," he added.
The government's Economic Planning Agency (EPA) said it will announce the gross domestic product (GDP) data for October to December period on Thursday.

A Reuters poll of economists produced an average forecast for growth in Japan's real GDP of 0.8 percent quarter-on-quarter for the three months to December, up from 0.1 percent growth in the previous quarter. The forecasts ranged from 0.3 percent to 1.2 percent growth.

Economists said the data would show that private consumption and external demand were the twin engines propelling growth in the fourth quarter of 1996. They said a drop in public works spending was the biggest factor in hampering growth.

Low interest rates and a scheduled increase in Japan's sales tax to five percent from the current three percent on April 1 will have accelerated growth in housing investment in the period, economists said.
The scheduled tax increase also helped encourage automobile sales during the quarter, economists said.
They said private consumption would show a rebound from especially low growth in the previous quarter, which was due to a food poisoning epidemic.

Companies had yet to discard their cautious outlook on the economy, but corporate capital spending would show an increase in the quarter as the tax increase encouraged continued purchases of machinery before April, the economists said.

Exports received a push from the weakness of the yen, which boosted the competitiveness of Japanese products abroad and tempered the flood of imports coming into Japan. Strong demand, especially in the United States boosted car exports, they said.
Public works spending, which fuelled the economic recovery in its early stages, would show a considerable drop in October-December period, the economists said.

"What was alloted (as an economic stimulus package) for public works spending in the supplementary budget in fiscal 1995/96 was exhausted in the October-December quarter," said Nomura Research Institute economist Kyohei Morita.
Economists expect GDP growth in calendar 1996 to be more than three percent and that for the fiscal year to March 1997 to more or less meet the government forecast of 2.5 percent.

Fiscal tightening measures -- in the form of the sales tax increase, an end to special income tax cuts, and an increase in social security charges -- would have the effect of cutting GDP by more than one percent in 1997/98, economists said.
Japan's forecast for real GDP for 1997/98 is 1.9 percent. Some economists considered the forecast realistic while others doubted Japan would be able to achieve it.

Some economists expect exports to contribute substantially to growth, but others disagreed, saying many firms were moving production overseas and that foreign demand, especially from the United States, was expected to slacken in coming months.

"These measures will have an impact on the economy, but not so much as to push the current gradual economic recovery into recession. It's just that the pace of the recovery is going to become slower," said Yozo Nishimura, an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, Ltd.
